title: Neutron Stars, Pulsars, and Magnetars
executive_summary: A neutron star is the collapsed core of a massive supergiant star. They are the smallest and densest stellar objects known, compressing ~1.4 to 2.1 solar masses into a sphere only 10–12 km in radius.
image_caption: The Crab Nebula, containing the famous central Crab Pulsar.

key_sections.title: Nuclear Density Matter
key_sections.content: Neutron star matter is so dense that a single sugar-cube volume weighs over 400 million tons on Earth. At these densities, free electrons are forced into protons via neutronization, creating a sea of pure neutrons.

key_sections.title: Pulsars: Cosmic Lighthouses
key_sections.content: Pulsars are highly magnetized, rapidly rotating neutron stars emitting beams of electromagnetic radiation from their magnetic poles. As they spin, sweeping radiation beams cross Earth at ultra-precise regular intervals.

key_sections.title: Magnetars: Ultra-Strong Magnetic Fields
key_sections.content: Magnetars are a subclass of neutron stars possessing magnetic field strengths up to 10^15 Gauss (100 billion Tesla)—the strongest magnetic fields in the Universe, capable of causing starquakes and powerful gamma-ray bursts.
